Question: Is it time to reject the oft repeated claim by idiots that hydrogen from electrolysis is inefficient? It isn't. Its about as efficient as an electrical transformer now, above 95% efficient as described in the link in my comment.
Answer: Hydrogen isn’t a source of energy, it is a method of storing energy. To understand the worth of hydrogen for storing energy you need to include (1) its production which is what electrolysis does, (2) where the electricity comes from in producing it, (3) the method of containing and transporting it, (4) how it is used, and finally, (5) how that compares with other methods of storing energy. Yes, (1) its production from electricity is efficient. But that’s just one factor of several.

Question: Can empty relations be reflexive, symmetric, etc.?
Answer: The empty relation on a nonempty set is symmetric and transitive, but it’s not reflexive. The empty relation on the empty set is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. It’s an equivalence relation. You can verify those statements using only the definitions of reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

Question: How can we give an example of a non-abelian group such that every subgroup of G is normal in G?
Answer: There’s a name for non-Abelian groups for which all their subgroups are normal. Dedekind called them Hamiltonian groups in honor of Hamilton who introduced quaternions. In fact, the smallest Hamiltonian group is the quaternion group Q 8 which has eight elements. Dedekind studied these groups at the end of the 19th century. Of course, every subgroup of an Abelian group is normal, but he wondered what other subgroups have this property. He proved that all of them involve Q 8 somehow. In particular each Hamiltonian group is the direct product of Q 8 and an Abelian group A . Not every Abelian group A works to make Q 8 × A a Hamiltonian group, and Dedekind characterized which ones do.

Question: How can we explain what a binary relation is to someone who doesn't know math?
Answer: Examples are a good way to give someone a good idea. What are some binary relations that concern people? One is motherhood. To say x is the mother of y defines a binary relation on the set of people. For any two people, either x is the mother of y or x is not the mother of y . Others are fatherhood, sisterhood, and brotherhood. There are loads of others like x is taller than y , x is older than y , x is a good friend of y . Those are all binary relations on the set of people. Likewise, you can have binary relations on sets of other things like words, atoms, countries, and anything else you can name. It isn’t necessary that binary relations relate only things that belong to the same set. You can have a binary relation between people and clothing apparel, as, for example, x is wearing y . All these binary relations relate two things. There are other relations that relate other numbers of things. Unary relations are only about one thing. If you’re talking about the set of animals, then doghood is a unary relation, for any animal, either x is a dog or x is not a dog. There are also ternary relations that relate three things. I’ve been thinking about a certain quaternary relation, proportion. It relates four things. You can express it as w is to x as y is to z . . Binary relations are important, though, since so many common relations are binary, equality being the most common binary relation.
